articles.title: Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17
articles.author: Ben Schoon
articles.content:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.
What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?
One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8.
Some key changes in One UI 9 include:
- Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu
- Broader support for Now Nudge
- My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject
- More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization
- AI privacy alerts
- Upgrades to Samsung DeX
- New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper
Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list
While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.
Galaxy S devices with Android 17
- Galaxy S26
- Galaxy S26+
- Galaxy S26 Ultra
- Galaxy S25 (rolling out more widely)
- Galaxy S25+ (rolling out more widely)
- Galaxy S25 Ultra (rolling out more widely)
- Galaxy S25 FE (limited availability)
- Galaxy S25 Edge (limited availability)
- Galaxy S24 (limited availability)
- Galaxy S24+ (limited availability)
- Galaxy S24 Ultra (limited availability)
Galaxy Z devices with Android 17
- Galaxy Z Fold 7 (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z Flip 7 (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z TriFold (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z Fold 6 (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z Flip 6 (limited availability)
Galaxy A devices with Android 17
- Galaxy A57 (limited availability)
Updating…
One UI 9 changelog
Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.
Galaxy AI
Enhanced Now nudge
- Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.
Focus on someone important
- My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.
Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you
- In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.
See useful information during calls
- See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.
Productivity and multitasking
More customizable quick panel
- You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.
Privacy, security, and device protection
Warranty and care
- The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.
Lock down your phone quickly
- It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.
Location access transparency
- Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.
Stronger security and privacy protection
- Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.
AI privacy alerts
- Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.
Samsung Health
New look for Samsung Health
- Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.
Customize your Health home screen
- Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.
Log health data quickly
- It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.
Advanced trend analysis
- Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.
Monitor changes in your sleep vitals
- Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.
Manage your heart health
- Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.
Track your cardio load
- See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.
Check your fitness index
- Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.
Keep your ears safe
- The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.
View your cycle and body rhythm
- Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.
Bixby
Activate Bixby with a gesture
- Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.
Manage your conversations
- Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.
Bixby on the Home screen
- Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.
Accessibility
Discover new Accessibility features
- Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.
Text spotlight for easier reading
- Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.
Physical keyboard shortcuts
- Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.
Mouse keys enhancements
- New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.
Replace swipe with single tap
- The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.
Select to speak
- Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.
Improved TalkBack updates
- TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.
Even more improvements
New Lock screen clock
- The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.
Samsung DeX enhancements
- It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.
Follow Ben: Twitter/X, Threads, Bluesky, and Instagram

articles.summary:
Samsung has begun the global rollout of its One UI 9 update, bringing Android 17 features and enhanced AI-powered tools to a wide range of Galaxy smartphones and tablets.

### Key Points
- The update introduces My FanCam for automatic subject tracking in videos and expanded Now Nudge suggestions for notifications and maps.
- New privacy features include AI-driven permission monitoring and a quick-lock mechanism accessible via physical buttons or the Quick Panel.
- Samsung Health has been redesigned with improved trend analysis, cardio load tracking, and a customizable home screen for health metrics.
- Bixby now supports gesture-based activation, allowing users to trigger the assistant by raising the phone without using a wake-up word.
- The update is currently available for the Galaxy S26, S25, and S24 series, as well as various Z Fold, Z Flip, and A-series devices.

### Why it Matters
This update represents a significant software evolution for Samsung, prioritizing AI-driven productivity and user privacy across its mobile ecosystem. By integrating deeper health analytics and streamlined security controls, Samsung aims to maintain its competitive edge in the premium smartphone market.

articles.title: Why Is There A Lock Symbol Next To Your Text Messages?
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Suzanne Bonnett)
articles.content:
Why Is There A Lock Symbol Next To Your Text Messages?
Spotting a random unfamiliar lock symbol right next to your private text messages might feel like something to be alarmed about, especially with scam texts on the rise. But really, there's no reason to panic. Your phone hasn't been hacked, and your carrier hasn't all of a sudden locked your account down or anything like that. This little lock symbol actually means that your chats are secure. Think of it basically as a real-time status indicator that provides evidence that end-to-end encryption is actively protecting that text message thread from unwanted snooping.
Think of end-to-end encryption as a digital safe that carries your texts across the internet. When you send a text, this encryption essentially scrambles the words into an unreadable tangle of code. The message travels across cellular networks and server farms while staying in this locked form, and the only device with the ability to easily unlock and read that message is your recipient's phone. Because of this strict lock-and-key setup, even if someone intercepts your message, they won't be able to read it (at least not easily). Generally speaking, cellular providers can't read the messages, and even the tech companies that host the platform can't read anything. The padlock symbol simply lets you know that your private jokes, photos, and any other content you send in there are shielded from prying eyes.
Managing encryption on an Android device
For anyone using an Android smartphone, Google Messages is usually the default texting app. If you're texting a friend who also uses Google Messages (and with a solid Wi-Fi connection), the app automatically upgrades your chat to Rich Communication Services, more commonly called RCS. This upgrade is what brings that padlock symbol into play. A tiny lock symbol pops up on the send button and next to message timestamps, confirming that the end-to-end encryption protocol is hard at work.
Keep in mind that this seamless privacy shield only works when both devices play by the same rules. If a text goes out to an older phone or a device with a bad data connection, the system tries to deliver the message using RCS, then downgrades to old-school SMS messaging if that fails. The lock icon goes away, warning you that any future messages won't be secure against outside interception until you're back on RCS.
While keeping this encryption active is a smart move for digital safety, some users prefer standard texts for network reliability in rural areas, despite there being reasons you shouldn't use SMS messages. Disabling this security feature requires shutting off RCS completely. To do so, just open Google Messages, tap your profile picture at the top right, and dive into the settings menu. Tap on the RCS chats option and flip the toggle switch off. The lock icon will vanish from all future chats.
How Apple handles secure messaging
Apple handles digital security differently, keeping everything tightly integrated into its own software. Instead of sticking a padlock next to every single text, iOS uses a color system to show text security status. When there's a conversation between two Apple devices using iMessage, the text bubbles are blue; these blue bubbles are Apple's indicators that your chat is locked down with its own system-level end-to-end encryption.
In 2024, Apple finally decided to adopt the modern RCS standard for texting people outside its ecosystem, and it made a deliberate choice: it kept the green bubbles. For Apple, green simply means the message is traveling outside of its walled garden. For a long time, texting a green bubble meant those messages were unencrypted. Apple refused to use Google's proprietary RCS standard, waiting instead for a universal industry standard to be finalized. Now that one exists, Apple and Google are finally rolling out end-to-end encryption for those cross-platform chats. Despite Apple keeping green bubbles, they're now just as secure as its well-known blue bubbles, especially for iPhones chatting with select Android users.
The iPhone still operates within strict boundaries, though, just like Android. If a text gets sent to an older smartphone, or a device struggling with a bad data connection, the phone automatically ditches the advanced network and falls back to a standard SMS message once an RCS message send fails. To turn off RCS on your iPhone, head to Settings, then Apps, and then tap Messages. From there, click into the Text Messaging section, then tap RCS Messaging, and toggle that switch off.
articles.summary:
The appearance of a padlock icon next to text messages indicates that end-to-end encryption is active, ensuring that conversations remain private and protected from unauthorized interception.

### Key Points
- The padlock symbol confirms that messages are scrambled into unreadable code, accessible only by the sender and the intended recipient.
- On Android devices, the lock icon appears in Google Messages when Rich Communication Services (RCS) is enabled for secure, encrypted chats.
- Apple uses blue bubbles to denote encrypted iMessage conversations, while green bubbles now also support encryption when using the universal RCS standard.
- Encryption automatically disables if a device lacks a stable data connection, causing the app to revert to standard, unencrypted SMS messaging.
- Users can manually disable RCS in the settings menu of either Google Messages or the iPhone Messages app to stop using encrypted protocols.

### Why it Matters
Understanding these security indicators helps users distinguish between encrypted chats and standard SMS messages that are vulnerable to interception. As platforms like Apple and Google adopt universal standards, this encryption provides a consistent layer of privacy for cross-platform communication.

articles.title: LLMs Aren't Inevitable
articles.author: Iris Meredith
articles.content:
About as common as the statement that AI technology is just a tool is the statement that AI is "inevitable", so we should all just give up and get with the program because the technology is definitely going to persist and we're definitely going to give up our thinking to the machines. This is obviously a thought-terminating cliche, but it's work digging into a little further: after all, given how much it's being said, it would be worth knowing exactly how and why it's wrong.
The idea of a technology being "inevitable" is a curious one: after all, nobody knows ahead of time what technologies are going to be developed or adopted by society, so you certainly can't say, for example, that workable nuclear fusion generation is inevitable: that would be foolish. Equally, in hindsight any technology that is widely adopted and popular could be said to be inevitable: you get no points for saying that the development of the iPhone was "inevitable", not the least because we don't actually know if that's true for the shape the technology took. It's probably true for something with the vague shape of the technology in question, but it could have taken any number of forms, including a bunch that we'd probably think are quite strange.
So what is meant by inevitable when AI boosters say it? And how does AI measure up by their implicit standards?
What does it mean for a technology to be "inevitable"?
The glib response here would be to say that no technology is ever inevitable and that everything is contingent. This has the advantages of being technically true and sounding wise, but unfortunately technologies very much exist that a reasonable person might well label that way. Firearms are a good example of the latter case: once they've been developed, you quite quickly hit the situation where if you want to maintain your independence and safety in a society, you have to either use one or have one used on your behalf: no other options really work.
The inevitability of a technology is not, however, a factor of the technology alone. After all, mesoamerican civilisations very much understood the wheel as a technology. However, in dense jungle and without a road network already existing, wheels aren't actually hugely useful: it's thus no surprise that mesoamerican civilisations primarily relied on water transport and pack animals and relegated wheels largely to toys for children. More saliently, the value of cannon as a military technology was significantly greater in Europe, where political fragmentation led to fortifications being built with tall, thin walls designed to resist escalade, than they were in China, where stone-faced walls built largely of rammed earth were the norm (a cannon can blast a breach in the first much faster than it can in the second, though it will eventually breach both).
The inevitability of a technology is thus, in itself, a thing that is contingent on social and cultural structures: the same technology might prove to be "inevitable" in one cultural sphere, completely useless in another and useful but far from being "inevitable" in a third. Our criteria for "inevitability" relative to a given culture might thus look roughly as follows.
A technology is inevitable if:
- The technology can perform a task to a standard equal or not markedly inferior to that of an alternative technology doing the same task.
- The task in question is socially valuable: we need a lot of it done, and it's currently done by labour that is, in some sense, scarce
- The technology can, in volume of adequate output or in quality of output, overwhelmingly outclass what alternative technologies can do. A moderate improvement isn't really enough to force inevitability: it has to be a massive difference.
- There's no way in which the people not using the technology can change their behaviour to neutralise the impact of the technology. Firearms were overwhelming in this sense while the counterweight trebuchet wasn't because, while it's essentially impossible to mitigate the impact of cannon without radical changes to how fortifications are built, a counterweight trebuchet can have its impact blunted with incremental changes.
Unless all of these conditions hold, the adoption of a given technology can be fairly held to be contingent and not inevitable: it's not a choice that a social grouping was forced into, but one that they chose relatively freely. In short, inevitable technologies are ones where, if you don't adopt them, you will swiftly be overwhelmed by the cultures and societies that do. This seems to me to be largely in keeping with the way that LLM advocates use the term: LLM technology is inevitable because people who don't use it will fall so far behind those that do in power that they will end up under the control of LLM users.
Looking at this, we can quite clearly see the pattern of inevitability when it comes to gunpowder. A cannon can breach a curtain wall much faster than a counterweight trebuchet, and more efficiently too. Breaching curtain walls is something that, in a fragmented mediaeval Europe, is very socially valuable: if you can breach a wall, you can take a city or a castle, and the faster you do that, the less time you have to spend laying siege. Cannon is overwhelmingly more powerful than other kinds of siege equipment, and even early small arms were able to deliver overwhelmingly more energy in a shot than an equivalent crossbow or longbow could. Finally, there wasn't any particularly easy way to neutralise firearms: they're very difficult to effectively armour against and while you can design fortifications that are effective against cannon, the labour inputs required for that demand a massive restructuring of society. Practically speaking, then, the moment cannon arrived in Europe, militaries found themselves in a situation where they had to adopt firearms technology as quickly as possible or else be absorbed into the state of someone who had. That, I think, is what we colloquially mean by a technology being "inevitable".
We might compare this, for purposes of discussion, against the magnetic compass. The magnetic compass meets the first two criteria: it works a hell of a lot better for finding north than taking sightings of the sun and calculating does, and it works even absent known landmarks. Moreover, knowing the direction of north is rather useful when you're a maritime power and want to be able to navigate effectively. However, it's not overwhelmingly efficient: you can still navigate effectively without one, and it's easy enough to neutralise simply by virtue of not taking an interest in maritime activities and becoming a land power. Thus, while the magnetic compass allowed the colonial powers of Europe to massively extend their reach and exploit resources that would otherwise have been unavailable, Russia, for example, would likely have become and remained a major power on the continent whether they had the magnetic compass or not. The compass, then, while it was a very powerful and useful technology, was not inevitable in the way that firearms were.
Are modern LLMs inevitable?
So how does modern AI (in the LLM sense) measure up against these standards?
The first point is the question of whether an LLM can do work not markedly inferior to that of a human doing the same task or not. This one is debatable. An LLM absolutely cannot produce work to the highest human standards, or even a good human standard at the moment, and it's unlikely that it ever will. Most human work, however, is not done at a good standard. At best it's mediocre, and at worst it's downright horrible. The bulk of human knowledge work done in an awful of settings, then, is unfortunately more or less interchangeable with that of an LLM (seriously, so much human work is just awful: I wish I could say otherwise). On this point, then, LLMs probably pass the criterion.
The next question is that of social value. A lot of the knowledge work that LLMs purport to replace is scarce and valued: the writing of software, research work, graphic design and so forth. Generally, however, the LLM can only replace the least valuable parts of that work, to a greater or lesser degree (an LLM can generate a meaningful volume of tolerably mediocre code, but only the very worst kinds of graphic design and fairly superficial research documents). This means that, when any level of real quality is required, human expertise will have to be involved, whether an LLM is being used or not. On this question, then, the results are mixed: LLMs can do socially meaningful work, but only to an extent, and the more socially important the work is, the less useful LLMs are for it.
Now we come to the question of whether or not the difference that LLMs bring to the table is sufficiently overwhelming to make their adoption inevitable, and on this I think the answer is a clear no. As established above, LLMs just can't do top-flight work at all: at the heights of basically any discipline, we're still very much relying on unaugmented human work. Even at lower levels of accomplishment, LLMs still aren't overwhelmingly powerful: even when an LLM is being used, the amount of effort that goes into making sure that the LLM is directed correctly and that the output is adequate to the task means that the volume of output is sharply restricted. This means that while you might get some more output from using an LLM than you might without it in some cases, the actual speed-up isn't drastic. You might be getting between 20% and 50% more PowerBI dashboards out of an LLM-enhanced workflow than you would without LLMs, but the dashboards are likely not a core bottleneck in your business in any case, and as of now, at least, it seems that the closer you get to those core bottlenecks the fewer efficiency gains you see. Either way, I cannot help but feel that if there were a real overmatch in capability, we would very much have seen it so far. There would be at least one tech company producing five to ten times as many new tech products as anyone else and slowly forcing everyone else out of the market. We have not seen this: in fact, what we have seen is that the companies that have been going all in on AI have been struggling more than the others. The overwhelming levels of real impact that we would have had to see (think tanks rolling through the Ardennes Forest, crewed by methed-up Wehrmacht) to conclude that the technology must inevitably adopted... it simply isn't there.
Finally there's the question of whether or not there are things that other people can do to neutralise the impact of the technology relatively cheaply. There's not much evidence for this one way or another at the moment because social trends take a while to shake out, but in the forms of social competition that our societies tend to engage with, I'm inclined to say that there absolutely are. The level of social opprobrium directed at LLM use and at people attempting to pass off generated slop as work is immense, and that cannot but have, in the long run, negative impacts on the technology. In general, new technologies need some level of social acceptance in order to be adopted, and while many technologies have been adopted in the face of indifference or mild dislike, very few have been adopted in the face of the kind of white-hot hatred that's directed at LLMs at present. Moreover, we aren't talking about John Henry and the steel-driving machine here: in terms of actual useful output, humans can still match an LLM quite comfortably even if an LLM outmatches us in terms of sheer volume.
On these criteria of inevitability, then, LLMs don't come out very well. They only really pass on one criterion, and that incompletely. Moreover, on the criteria that push a technology from being merely useful to truly inevitable (criteria 3 and 4), the LLMs absolutely fail to get anywhere. Whatever the utility of LLM tools is, then, it seems clear that LLMs as such fall entirely in the category of contingence rather than inevitability.
This isn't an end to it, however, because we can clearly see that LLMs are having a massive impact over large swathes of our current social situation. Even if the technology, by the standpoints given above, isn't inevitable, it certainly feels, to a lot of people, as though it is. Why is that?
LLMs as chemical weapons
In his work Why don't we use chemical weapons any more?, Bret Devereaux discusses the question of why, since World War I, top-flight militaries have almost never used chemical weapons in battlefield applications. What's immediately striking is that this is basically true: despite the development of increasingly potent nerve agents such as Sarin, VX and Novichok, these have almost never seen battlefield use by the great powers. Neither Soviet Russia or Nazi Germany used them during World War Two, despite both of these powers being pushed to levels of desparation that would likely have resulted in their use having happened had they been at all effective. They weren't used in Vietnam or Korea (despite superficially similar defoliant agents being used), and while there have been some reports of Russia using chemical weapons in the Russo-Ukrainian war (mostly, as it seems, as a kind of pro-forma atrocity), reports of them being used in any serious way that enabled Russian battlefield gains are almost entirely absent. Given the sheer lethality of these agents, then, one might ask the question of why they've not become inevitable technologies that we cannot avoid using in war, however immoral their use might be.
Devereaux's answer to this is that for top-flight armies operating on modern manuever warfare principles, the great lethality of chemical weapons does not, in fact, translate to great utility. Modern manuever warfare, after all, relies on a great deal of tactical mobility on the attack, aiming to move fast enough to isolate and disorient resistance, preventing a co-ordinated defence and causing defending forces to collapse. In such a situation, the last thing you want is to use munitions that make large areas impassable to both you and your enemy, which chemical weapons inevitably do. Adding to this issue is the fact that more or less complete protection against chemical agents (gas mask plus NBC suit) is, by the standards of a modern economy, remarkably cheap: as Devereaux phrases it, there's a good chance that complete protection against this kind of weapon is cheaper than a soldier's rifle, and a wealthy country can, if it chooses, basically give its entire population protection against chemical attacks. And besides that, modern explosives are arguably more lethal in a battlefield situation, weight-for-weight, than almost any chemical agent (in principle, the lethal dose of a chemical agent is very low, but actually getting someone to be exposed to a sufficient dose of a chemical agent on a battlefield is a crapshoot at best: five litres of sarin in the Tokyo Subway attacks only actually killed twelve people, despite the situation being about as favourable for a chemical attack as you can get). This means that if you have an army capable of modern-system manuever warfare, whether you're fighting another modern-system army or a static-system army (to use Devereaux's terminology), chemical weapons are basically useless to you.
If you're a weak power fighting another weak power, though, chemical weapons can be quite useful. After all, if none of these points hold, using the technology might well make sense, as we saw during the Iran-Iraq war. Similarly, chemical weapons might be used in terror attacks or to send a message (Sergei Skripal's poisoning in London seems to have fallen into this category). Notably, however, you're only going to use this technology if you are, in one sense or another, a weaker power: you don't have the budget, the will or the skills to do modern manuever warfare. In general, chemical weapons are an excellent object lesson in why a supposedly very capable, effective technology is far from being inevitable and is in fact highly culturally contingent in terms of whether or not it's useful. And, to be clear, it's obviously wrong to say that the widespread adoption of chemical weapons is inevitable in our sense: one might perhaps say that it's inevitable that the technology will persist (it's impossible, after all, to un-invent a technology), but it's clearly not inevitable that advanced militaries will inevitably make and use the devices.
Now, to the point of this article: it's my contention that LLMs more or less fall into the same technological category as LLMs when it comes to their inevitability. Chemical weapons, after all, fall out roughly the same way as LLMs in our earlier categorisation: they can do some things in a military context, sometimes better than equivalent conventional weapons, but they're not overwhelmingly better than conventional weapons, they're often way worse and they're trivial to neutralise.
The inevitability of LLMs, therefore, is of a piece with the inevitability of chemical weapons. Weak players who are fighting other weak players might well find some use for them. I suspect that we're going to be seeing second or third rate software engineering shops using these tools (whether they're the hyperscaler models or local models) for a very long time. For them, the primary concern is volume of crap put out, and the functionality of what's produced is at best a secondary concern (Shopify and Mailchimp are barely-functional pieces of shit and were so before LLMs became widespread, but they've always been quite competitive at the lower levels of their respective applications). People and companies who are at all serious, however, are likely to use them only a little or not at all (the pattern I've noted among people who use the technology whom I'd consider serious is very different from other use , and also generally much lower in magnitude even for the heavy users), and if the pattern we see with chemical weapons holds, those companies will massively outclass what the bulk of the competition is able to do. Similarly, LLMs might have meaningful applications in hybrid warfare, as in the use of chemical weapons as a terror weapon (the recent rise of LLM-backed cyberattacks and LLM astroturfing bots genuinely concerns me), but remain uncompetitive when it comes to actually doing work of substance. I think we see both of these patterns come up frequently enough that I strongly suspect this is going to be the pattern going forwards, at least in the near future.
Certainly, given that situation you might say that LLMs are inevitable in the weak sense: inevitable in the sense that we can't uninvent the technology and that there are going to be weak actors that will persist in using the tools. In the strong sense, however? Certainly not. Any actor that's at all serious in their field is, sooner or later, going to hit a point where LLMs cease being useful to them and actively hinder their further progress, and we absolutely do not see the massively overwhelming advantages that LLMs would need to have in order to become inevitable.
The question of how our future looks going forward, I think, depends on our last point: how well can we neutralise the effects that LLMs are having on our situation? If we cannot find a way to effectively make it difficult for LLMs to hurt us, the situation is likely to be one where LLM adoption isn't inevitable, but it'll continue for largely contingent reasons. After all, most combats in our society (so to speak) are conflicts of weak parties against weak parties, and if the LLM cannot be effectively neutralised LLM technology can still act as an effective deterrent against stronger powers. People doing things for whom LLMs are useless will still be able to hold their own, but they won't have enough of an overwhelming advantage over LLM users that they can make LLM usage prohibitive. This is, unfortunately, quite a bleak world: it's a world where there is still space for real skill and care, but also one where a significant minority of the population is stuck pointing LLMs at each other and rotting their brains away in the process, the consequences of which we'll all have to deal with: a well-poisoning situation in which we all have to dedicate significant effort to filtering the LLM crud out that could be spent on something else.
If, however, we can neutralise the LLM threat somehow (perhaps by some combination of regulation, economics and social opprobrium), there is considerable hope. If we can mitigate the effects that LLMs have on us and reduce the filtering burden, we can, more likely than not, simply outcompete LLM users. After all, LLMs, as we've previously established, are mostly useful to people who are not good at what they do: weak players in our socioeconomic game. LLMs are, at present, mostly allowing them to partially keep their heads above water relative to relatively skilled practitioners. And I think there is hope that we can neutralise that effectively. A large part of why LLM users are able to hold their own against strong players, for the moment, is that there's considerable belief in the power and potency of LLMs: a belief that is convenient for a lot of people but also fundamentally irrational. The idea that LLMs can do everything a human can only better, or even that it can lead to massive productivity gains, is already eroding. We can speed that erosion, and the moment that the belief erodes enough, the people who don't use LLMs because they already outclass them suddenly develop a crushing competitive advantage. I don't know when this will happen: it might take a few years, or even as long as a decade. But eventually I think this belief is quite likely to collapse.
Looking at all of this, the idea that LLMs are in some sense "inevitable" is more than a little foolish. Certainly, the technology we will always have with us. Certainly, the astroturfing bots are not going to go away. But is this technology overwhelmingly powerful enough that we all need to be using it now lest we fall under the power of people who do?
Nope.
Arca is my project to help maintain the skills and knowledge that we need to outclass the LLM users. We're in very early days yet, but the platform is available in early access, so if you're interested, please sign up and help me realise the project in full and keep me fed and housed while I do so.
articles.summary:
The widespread adoption of large language models is not an inevitable technological progression, but rather a contingent choice that fails to meet the criteria for overwhelming competitive necessity.

### Key Points
- A technology is only "inevitable" if it provides massive, unavoidable advantages that force competitors to adopt it or face obsolescence.
- Historical examples like firearms demonstrate true inevitability, whereas tools like the magnetic compass remained useful but optional.
- LLMs currently lack the capability to perform high-level, complex work, limiting their utility to mediocre or low-stakes tasks.
- The author compares LLMs to chemical weapons, which persist as niche tools for weak actors but offer no strategic advantage to high-performing organizations.
- Social resistance and the high cost of filtering AI-generated "slop" may eventually neutralize the perceived benefits of LLM integration.

### Why it Matters
- Understanding the limitations of AI helps businesses avoid over-investing in tools that provide only marginal efficiency gains rather than true competitive superiority. By recognizing that LLMs are not an inevitable replacement for human expertise, organizations can prioritize high-quality, human-led work to maintain a distinct market advantage.

articles.title: Ben Affleck’s ‘Ethical AI’ Vehicle Failing To Impress Human Viewers
articles.author: Zack Kotzer
articles.content:
Like Matt Damon’s dance with cryptocurrency before him, Ben Affleck’s flirtations with AI have developed into a full romance. The actor and director has been advocating for AI in Hollywood entertainment for over a year. Released this weekend, his Netflix feature Animals appears to be a vehicle for his envisioned “ethically” utilized AI. Though the end result doesn’t seem to be impressing viewers.
Starring and directed by Affleck, Animals follows Mark Kimball, a mayoral candidate lagging in the polls. When his son is taken hostage, Mark and his wife Abigail (Scandal’s Kerry Washington) attempt to source the ransom without sinking his chances in a close election.
While Affleck has directed a number of praised thrillers, from Gone Baby Gone to Academy Award winner Argo, critics haven’t taken as kindly to this political caper, citing paper thin personalities and clunky dialogue. The online peanuts gallery have also latched on to some abnormal looking shot composition, which look like the kind of clips Paul Rudd would present on Conan. The film is currently underwater on both critic and audience Rotten Tomato scores.
 سبب كافي يخليك تكره فلم ابن أفليك الجديد ANIMALS pic.twitter.com/3v2ap1fjMS
— غاس | FHD (@FHD_GUS) October 9, 2026
What Affleck opted to use AI for in the production of Animals is unclear, as the star has been coy about the process. What he does tout is that he wants AI to be used, in his mind, responsibly. Not breaching creative rights or intellectual property, or threatening anyone in Hollywood’s livelihoods. After being spooked by the tech years ago, he sees this as a way to keep humans at the table.
“I don’t believe that there will ever be ‘Just type it in and make a movie that people want to see,'” said Affleck at a recent Bloomberg event. “The whole effort behind it was to do something ethical, to do something that did not displace people, but that allowed people in this economy and this world to benefit from this technology.”
Shaken as he may be, and despite all the rattling, Hollywood’s human entertainers have yet to be displaced by AI. Higher ups may be champing at the bit to displace headcounts and devalue labor, but audiences are overwhelmingly lining up for art with that human touch, such as Kane Parsons’ simulacra lampooning Backrooms. AI is excellent at reminding us about its existence at every turn, but less effective at motivating a ticket sale.
articles.summary:
Ben Affleck’s new Netflix thriller Animals has received poor critical reception as audiences scrutinize the director’s controversial decision to incorporate AI technology into the film’s production process.

### Key Points
- Animals stars Ben Affleck and Kerry Washington as parents navigating a political kidnapping plot during a mayoral campaign.
- The film is currently struggling with low critic and audience scores on Rotten Tomatoes due to complaints regarding dialogue and visual composition.
- Affleck has publicly advocated for the "ethical" use of AI in Hollywood to assist creators without displacing human labor or violating intellectual property.
- Despite his advocacy, the specific technical applications of AI used during the production of Animals remain undisclosed by the director.

### Why it Matters
The negative reception of Animals highlights a growing tension between Hollywood’s push for AI integration and audience demand for authentic, human-led storytelling. This project serves as a high-profile test case for whether industry leaders can successfully balance emerging technology with the creative standards expected by viewers.

articles.title: HP EliteBook X G2i laptop review
articles.author: Alastair Jennings
articles.content:
TechRadar Verdict
I opened up the EliteBook X G2i and was surprised by just how lightweight this laptop feels, especially considering the power of the processor and integrated GPU and NPU. Sure enough, the test benchmarks highlighted just how well-tuned this laptop was for everyday tasks, but it was also capable of editing video as well as supporting AI-enhanced workloads within Photoshop and with Copilot. However, this power and discreet design all come with a hefty business-focused price tag.
Reasons to buy
- + Exceptionally light
- + Killer keyboard
- + Decent integrated graphics
- + High-resolution 3K display
- + Handles productivity and content creation
Reasons to avoid
- - Very expensive
- - Not designed for upgrades
- - Very business-focused
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
HP EliteBook X G2i: 30-second review
The EliteBook X G2i is deceptively lightweight due to the magnesium alloy that’s been used to make the outer casing, and as I’ve seen before with this material when it’s used in laptops, whilst the material itself is exceptionally strong, there is quite a bit of flex to it, which could be mistaken for a cheaper design.
However, the aesthetics back up the premium pricing of this business-focused laptop, and with its 14-inch screen and weight that comes in just below a kilo, it’s the perfect partner for anyone who travels frequently and needs a high-powered laptop to keep up with all their business dealings.
Inside is the latest Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, which is coupled with Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics, and of course there’s also an integrated NPU to enhance all the AI potential from Copilot and other applications.
This laptop is obviously business-focused. However, that B390 GPU packs in some serious power, and whilst it isn’t gaming-focused, if you do want some downtime on a business trip, then this is very capable of playing some of the latest games. Whilst you might have to dial down some of the graphics, you’ll still get decent gameplay backed up with pretty decent audio.
Checking over the body, there’s a select choice of inputs, including the full-size HDMI, so when you arrive at your destination you can plug into larger monitors or displays, including projectors for presentations. There are two Thunderbolt 4 ports that offer up to 40Gbps, so you can plug in larger external drives to expand on the relatively small 1TB internal SSD. On the right-hand side, there are two more ports: standard USB-A and a slower USB Type-C 3.2.
As I ran through the tests, first of all starting off with Microsoft Office, this laptop kept pace with opening Word documents, editing and updating spreadsheets, and creating PowerPoint presentations, and this was all well within the capabilities of this powerful laptop. What was especially relevant here was that 3K-resolution screen, which just gives you that extra bit of real estate so that, when it comes to laying out your work, you’re not struggling to see palettes or the presentation at full size.
As I swapped over to some creative applications, starting in Lightroom then progressing onto Photoshop, again the speed of this laptop really stood out. It handled Photoshop without issue, and Lightroom rendered libraries quickly. As I then progressed onto CapCut and then Premiere Pro for video editing. Whilst I did need to plug in an external SSD to boost the storage, the machine itself was more than capable of handling short 4K edits without missing a frame.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The only time the machine did start to show limitations was as I swapped over to playing games, and whilst it was capable of running Indiana Jones and the Great Circle and Hogwarts Legacy, as I started to crank up the graphics, I could start to see the frame rates struggle and the fans kick in. However, that said, using the standard settings set through the installation for these games, the gameplay was exceptionally good.
The power of this small machine is reflected in the price, and this is by no means cheap, especially when you consider it only has a 1TB hard drive and 32GB of RAM. When you go up to the next level, the price does dramatically increase.
However, I'd rate this as one of the best business laptops for those looking for a machine that goes well beyond everyday work. Yes, it supplies far more power than most people will require, but the balance of ability and cost is exceptionally well considered, and when you take into account just how powerful it is and just how lightweight, if you travel frequently, then this is a great option.
HP EliteBook X G2i: Price and availability
- How much does it cost? From £2,445 / $3,599
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Directly from HP or Amazon
At present, the HP EliteBook X G2i is available for £2,445.59 including VAT, and in the US, a similar configuration to the one that I’ve looked at here retails for around US$3,599. The laptop is widely available either directly through the HP website or through most major retailers, both on the high street and online.
- Value: 3.5 / 5
HP EliteBook X G2i: Specs
CPU: Intel Core Ultra X7 358H, 16 cores/16 threads, up to 4.8GHz
Graphics: Intel Arc B390 integrated GPU
RAM: 32GB LPDDR5x-9600 onboard
Storage: 1TB PCIe NVMe M.2 SSD
Display: 14-inch, 2880 x 1800, 120Hz, 500 nits, 100% DCI-P3
Left Ports: 2x Thunderbolt 4/USB-C 40Gbps, HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm audio combo
Right Ports: USB-C 10Gbps, USB-A 5Gbps, nano security-lock slot
Connectivity: Intel Wi-Fi 7 BE211 (2x2), Bluetooth 6
Audio: Poly Studio, four stereo speakers, dual microphones with AI noise reduction
Camera: 5MP IR AI camera with privacy shutter
HP EliteBook X G2i: Design
When it comes to design, the EliteBook X G2i is incredibly understated. It’s finished in a dark blue, which HP has called Atmospheric Blue, which does give it a premium look, although when you first pick up the laptop, the lightweight build and the slight flex that you get with all-magnesium-alloy cases are slightly in contrast to what you expect.
However, having spent a couple of weeks fully testing the EliteBook X G2i and carrying it in my backpack, I’ve been impressed by both its durability and its lightweight design, which is far lighter than my usual MacBook Pro M1 Max, yet the power is easily equal to what the Mac is capable of.
Whilst the overall machine does look relatively small, as you open up the lid it reveals the large 14-inch screen, which is impressive with its 3K resolution, offering 2880 x 1800 resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate. As I sat in a café typing up this review with a bright light streaming in behind me, I was also impressed with the 500-nit brightness and the non-reflective screen that made it exceptionally easy to see the applications, where I have found in the past that some other screens are just too reflective.
Through the test, I planned a small video edit and PowerPoint presentations to create, and having to create these on the move seemed like a perfect time to put the laptop to the test. A couple of points that I noticed as I headed out the door were that the 1 TB SSD, which is fine for PowerPoint and most business-focused productivity, is still relatively small.
As I needed to also edit a video shot on the DJI OSMO Pocket 4P, I packed a Thunderbolt 4 portable SSD just to expand on the internal storage. This is where this laptop and its design really start to come into their own. The power is more than adequate for most productivity, but with that CPU and GPU combo, it’s also an ideal option for light to midweight creative applications such as Adobe Lightroom, Photoshop and Premiere Pro.
The only downside is that 1 TB SSD is rather limited. However, with those two USB4/Thunderbolt 4 ports on the side of the machine, I was able to connect a larger Thunderbolt 4 SSD to expand the storage, and this is a far cheaper option than opting for the larger-capacity internal SSD when speccing out the machine. The other point that I really like is that the HDMI on the side is full-sized, so when I arrived at the office or was ready for a lecture, I was able to plug the laptop directly into the existing system without the need for any adapters.
While the laptop is small and lightweight and packs in plenty of power, the one thing that impressed me more than anything else about the laptop was the quality of the keyboard. This is one of the best typing keyboards that I have ever come across on a laptop. The actuation of the keys is precise, and it has just a feeling of absolute quality. The keyboard layout is also well thought out, and whilst the cursor keys in the bottom right are half-sized, it’s just a pleasure to use.
When it comes to design, rather than aesthetics, it has a high-quality premium look, and whilst when you pick it up it is lightweight due to the magnesium casing, which does offer a little bit of flex, it is ultimately also extremely robust, just reinforcing its price point and intended use as a high-powered business machine to be used anywhere.
- Design: 4 / 5
HP EliteBook X G2i: Features
The feature set of this business-focused laptop is impressive, with an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H at the heart of the machine. This offers 16 cores and 16 threads and a boost up to 4.8GHz, which is more than enough for any corporate work but is also good for creative use as well as a bit of light to moderate gaming. Graphics are supplied by an integrated Intel Arc B390 GPU.
This is one up from many that we see in this level and type of laptop, which does give everything a little bit more potential. My review sample was equipped with 32GB of LPDDR5X onboard RAM. This means that it’s soldered to the motherboard and can’t be upgraded, but this is plenty for most productivity and even for light to midweight creative image and video use, although you are starting to hit the limits with video editing, and 64GB is generally the preferred amount.
When it comes to storage capacity, there’s a 1 TB NVMe SSD. This is a decent balance considering the cost of the machine, and if you do need more for video or just to store data, then you can pick up a relatively large and fast portable SSD that can be plugged into the ultrafast Thunderbolt 4 ports on the side.
As I’ve seen with a lot of mini PCs and laptops recently, there’s also an integrated NPU, and this is the Intel AI Boost NPU that provides up to 50 TOPS of performance and essentially helps Copilot and Adobe applications run locally without requiring online services for their AI features. If you’re thinking of running a local LLM then you can, but at 32GB RAM the potential is limited.
Impressively, when it comes to connectivity, there’s Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, so they're the current generations for both wireless connectivity options. When it comes to more traditional wired connectivity, there are two Thunderbolt 4 ports, which really show the premium level of this machine, and these support up to 40Gbps, ideal if you need to do some video editing.
But video and creative content aside, if you have large documents that you need to transfer to the machine or from one portable drive to another, then again that 40Gbps connection will be extremely welcome. Those ports also enable USB charging and DisplayPort 2.1. On the other side of the machine, there’s a further 10Gbps USB-C connection and a USB-A port for older devices if you need to connect them. This is really great to see on this level of machine, especially with its business focus.
Most importantly for business use is the fact that it offers HDMI 2.1, so if you need to connect up to a monitor, display or projector, then the full-size HDMI is pretty standard, so you shouldn’t need any other adapters. Essentially, you’ve got two different forms of connecting to displays: Thunderbolt 4 or the more standard HDMI.
The internal speakers for the laptop are also a bit of a surprise, and they offer really good audio clarity, both when listening back to meeting presentations and for playing games and listening to music. I also found that these were good, clear and loud for video conference calls, and those I was speaking to were able to hear me nice and clearly.
One of the big features of this new HP laptop is the HP business security suite, and as you start up, you get access to the full suite and its features, which include HP Admin, Sure Click, Sure Recover, Sure Sense and Tamper Lock. These all need to be set up by yourself or your IT team, but to have them all featured here just shows once again the focus on security and business of this laptop.
- Features: 4.5 / 5

Getting started with the HP EliteBook was all straightforward enough, and as I lifted it from the box, the first thing that struck me was just how lightweight this laptop is. With its magnesium-alloy casing, it had a nice, premium feel. There is a little bit of flex on the top of the machine, which you often get with these lightweight metals. That can be a bit deceptive, since you would normally associate that with cheaper units. However, through the two weeks of solid testing of this laptop, it was very obvious just how durable it is despite that slight flex.
Once the laptop is powered on, I ran through the usual Windows 11 Pro setup, which should take between 10 and 20 minutes depending on the options that you select. It also enables Windows Hello, so you can open and access the laptop using your face rather than needing to type in a password. It’s then a case of setting up any applications that you want, and HP has included its security suite here as well, which prompts you at various stages to complete the setup.
The HP security suite essentially offers lots of different features, including malware threat protection, credential protection, a secure browser, OS resiliency, application persistence and other features. You do need to activate it and register, but for the first year it all seems to be free.
As I started out the test, loading Microsoft Office to check out productivity, and as the Windows Experience score of 8.9 highlighted, this laptop just takes all Windows applications in its stride. Opening up Word, PowerPoint and Excel, running all three and quickly switching between each was as fast as any laptop.
But what really stood out here was that 3K-resolution screen, which just gives you far greater real estate for all the panels, and whilst everything is obviously a little bit smaller on screen, you can see an awful lot. There’s really good, high-quality clarity to the visuals.
A quick run of Geekbench 6 and 7 highlighted just how fast the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H is, and really, for all productivity, this machine is right at the top of what you would need. This was once again reinforced by the PCMark score.
As I progressed from productivity to creative applications and looked at Adobe Lightroom and Photoshop, again the speed of the processor and GPU working together provided a great balance.
The extra resolution that the screen offers over the lower-resolution screens that you often see on this size of laptop really does make a difference, especially in Photoshop, where navigating panels was just that much easier. Opening multiple images open shot on the Canon EOS R5 C, the clarity of the images was exceptionally good, and I was impressed with the overall colour accuracy of the monitor.
The other point here was that, as I opened up Adobe Bridge to view the thumbnails of the images shot, the machine was able to render the thumbnails quickly. Whilst there was still some render time, it kept up with the pace of the scrolling, and there was no point where I had to wait for minutes for those thumbnails to appear.
Opening up palettes, layers and working on images with enhancements was absolutely no challenge to the CPU or GPU, and even when I utilised Generative Expand on a couple of images to take them from 16:9 to 21:9 aspect ratio, the machine was able to process those locally, and the results were exceptionally good.
My only point through editing was the lack of SSD space for images. However, that Thunderbolt port on the side, with a portable SSD connected, expanded the storage easily and cheaply. This storage was again utilised for video editing, as there’s just not enough space on that internal SSD to store much.
But with the Thunderbolt 4 connection offering 40Gbps, Premiere Pro was able to access the drive with speed for both media and caching, and short five-minute video edits were completed with absolute ease, including transitions and rendering.
The one surprise here was that the performance of the internal SSD was far slower than I expected, with read and write speeds around the 3,500MB/s mark, which, considering the premium price tag and the positioning of this laptop, was slower than I had expected, with most laptops these days offering at least 5,000 to 6,000MB/s.
However, for general productivity this speed is more than sufficient, and even for image editing and most video it will keep up with the speed. It’s only when multiple files are being accessed or transferred that you will start to see a slight slowdown.
To finish off the test, I loaded up Indiana Jones and the Great Circle and was pleased to see that, firstly, it loaded without issue, and the gameplay was pretty solid, with smooth motion and graphics, although some of the more advanced effects were turned down. Likewise, Hogwarts Legacy was equally impressive on speed, and again, whilst some of the effects were turned down, the overall quality of the animation and gameplay was superb.
This is a business-focused laptop, and that’s obvious from the aesthetics, design and weight, coming in at less than a kilo, which makes it a perfect option for travel. Whilst many lightweight laptops sit in the premium bracket they can also be underpowered, however, here the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H packs in far more power than much larger laptops, and from productivity to creative work and even gaming, this laptop was more than powerful enough to run them all.
The other point that really impressed me was the fact that there’s a good selection of ports, with Thunderbolt 4 being supplied over the usual USB4 Type-C, and full-size HDMI and a standard USB Type-A, which enable plenty of flexibility for connectivity wherever you are.
However, surprisingly, the feature that really stood out to me beyond anything else was the quality of the keyboard. It felt much nicer to type on and higher quality than I’ve seen on far more expensive laptops, and the typing experience was fluid and swift. For me, when you look at the price, specifications, and quality of the screen and keyboard, that makes this laptop an exceptionally good option for business.
- Performance: 4.5 / 5
HP EliteBook X G2i: Final verdict
This ultralight 14-inch business laptop is powered by Intel’s latest Core Ultra X7 358H processor and backed by Arc B390 graphics. Wow, this laptop is ultra-light. The performance has been levelled up, as there is plenty of power beyond simple office tasks, and whilst it’s perfect for all productivity, its abilities will also stretch to some relatively midweight creative use, including editing video and dealing with the latest AI tasks.
The EliteBook X G2i does sit at the premium end of the laptop range, especially when you consider that it just has 32GB of RAM and a one-terabyte internal SSD. However, the lightweight design is backed by some serious processing and graphics potential. When it comes to pure productivity, there are few other laptops at this price that can match it on power.
There are things that are limited, such as that upper limit of RAM and the storage capacity, and whilst the storage can be boosted due to the fact that it features two Thunderbolt 4 ports, the RAM will be a bit of a limitation if you are looking for a laptop that not only enables you to use all the Microsoft Office applications at the top of their performance but is also a very capable 4K video-editing machine.
Whilst it is able to edit 4K video with relative ease, the internal SSD is a limitation, as is the 32GB of RAM. However, for the lightweight use intended, it will be more than sufficient.
Essentially, what you have here is a very powerful laptop that matches the power that you would usually expect from something a lot larger and heavier, which makes this an ideal option for anybody who travels frequently and needs a powerful laptop that they can always carry with them.
Some of my early worries about the robustness of the build due to some slight flex in the casing were gradually dispelled, and it proved that the magnesium material was robust and strong after lasting out the test as I carried it around in my backpack for a couple of weeks. However, I would’ve preferred, for a laptop at this price, for that top casing just to be a little more rigid.
When you look at competitors at this end of the market, and at this price, the HP EliteBook X G2i is exceptionally well priced. But what gives it the edge is not the power but the keyboard, which I can say is one of the nicest keyboards that I’ve ever used.
Should I buy the HP EliteBook X G2i?
| Value | this is a business-focused laptop, and for its high-powered CPU and GPU, you are paying a premium. | 3.5 | 
| Design | exceptionally light and slim, perfect for travel, but there is some flex in the casing | 4 | 
| Features | well-balanced set of features for general use; however, for creative use I’d probably opt for the 64GB version. | 4.5 | 
| Performance | all-round excellent performance from the CPU, GPU and NPU for both productivity and creative use. | 4.5 | 
| Overall | if you need a robust, powerful, lightweight laptop for travel, then this is an exceptional option. | 4 | 
Buy it if...
Travel is essential
At just under a kilogram, the EliteBook is seriously lightweight, and packing in powerful components, it’s a great option for travel.
Graphics actually matter
The Intel Arc B390 graphics are exceptionally good and proved very capable for both creative use in Photoshop and Premiere Pro, as well as some 3D modelling and rendering within Blender.
Don't buy it if...
Value comes first
This is a business-focused machine, and with that focus come certain features and components that all command premium prices. You can get cheaper machines with just as powerful components for a lesser price.
Gaming is a priority
While the Arc B390 GPU is impressive for general and creative use, if you’re into gaming, then you are going to want a GPU with a little more power.

articles.title: Apple Announcing HomePod Mini 2 Next Week With These New Features
articles.author: Joe Rossignol
articles.content:
Apple reportedly plans to unveil a new HomePod mini as part of the "Welcome home" experience it announced for Tuesday, October 13. We expect the new HomePod mini to be announced in a press release shared on the Apple Newsroom website at around 9 a.m. Eastern Time on that day, and hands-on photos and videos should surface shortly afterwards.
The second-generation HomePod mini is rumored to feature a newer chip that enables Siri AI support (at least with a nearby iPhone), along with improved sound quality, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, and new color options, including pink and green. No major design changes are expected.
Coincidentally, the original HomePod mini also debuted on October 13 back in 2020, so there has been a six-year wait for a new model. The current HomePod mini is powered by the S5 chip that debuted in the Apple Watch Series 5 in 2019.
In June, the HomePod mini received a price increase. In the U.S., it now costs $129, up from $99.
articles.summary:
Apple is expected to announce a second-generation HomePod mini on October 13, featuring upgraded internal hardware, enhanced Siri capabilities, and new color options for the smart speaker lineup.

### Key Points
- The new HomePod mini will reportedly include an N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support and an updated Ultra Wideband chip.
- Hardware improvements are expected to enable better sound quality and expanded Siri AI functionality when paired with an iPhone.
- The device will likely be available in new color options, including pink and green, while maintaining the original design.
- The current HomePod mini model, which launched in 2020, recently saw its U.S. retail price increase from $99 to $129.

### Why it Matters
This update marks the first hardware refresh for the HomePod mini in four years, signaling Apple's continued investment in its smart home ecosystem. By integrating advanced connectivity and AI-ready chips, Apple aims to maintain competitiveness against other smart speaker manufacturers in the premium home audio market.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablet finally gives the iPad lineup some much needed competition
articles.author: Michael Burkhardt
articles.content:
This week, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of Alexa Tablets. They no longer run a proprietary OS with a custom App Store, and instead embrace Android with a stock feel – while offering the Play Store. It’s a big shift in direction for Amazon. The tablets also look quite beautiful, while previous Fire tablets have felt cheap. I think these have the opportunity to do quite well.
First and foremost, I want to make it quite clear that I’m not saying the iPad is doomed or anything remotely close to that. However, I do think the Alexa Tablet serves as a real form of iPad competition, which the iPad has generally lacked.
New Alexa tablets serve as strong competition
Amazon is putting a lot of care into these tablets that other Android manufacturers haven’t, and while these tablets come in at lower price points – they certainly punch above their weight class.
There are three Alexa Tablets to start off the lineup: an 8.7” model at $229, an 11” model at $329, and a 12” Pro model at $499. To me, the one in the middle is the most interesting.
It offers 8GB of RAM, a 90Hz display, a thin design, and a similarly sharp display. That compares to the budget iPad, which comes in $120 higher with less RAM, a lesser display, and a thicker design. Granted, the iPad has the A16 chip, which probably feels much faster than the MediaTek chip powering it. The iPad also starts at 128GB, compared to the 64GB on the Alexa Tablet. Once you upgrade the Alexa Tablet to 128GB, there’s only a $70 difference.
Hardware wise, the Alexa Tablets seem pretty competent. Obviously, Android on tablets isn’t going to be quite perfect, but given its tie in with Alexa and the fact that the tablet is priced quite well, I could see a lot of people wanting to buy these, even if they potentially would’ve considered iPads. Of course, one strong suit from Amazon is the Kindle experience, and these Alexa Tablets offer a reader mode that cuts blue light.
Wrap up
Only time will tell, but Amazon might make a pretty big dent into the tablet market with its new entries. Even the 12” Pro at $499 seems like a really worthwhile product. At the very least, I hope some strong competition means Apple will be less complacent with its iPad upgrades. For example, the iPad Air has largely only received chip upgrades since its last redesign in 2020.
Top comment by GoldScooter
If it’s a tablet running Android, it’s not competition for the iPad. The developer support still just isn’t there.
I’m personally excited to try one of these out and truly put it to the test. Right now, Amazon also offers 20% off with any trade-in, making it an even better deal.
What do you think of these new Alexa Tablets? Would you consider getting one of these for a friend or family member during the holiday season? Sound off in the comments.
